episode_thesis: Pile argues that the 2010s demand-starved regime (pinned rates, QE, negative stock-bond correlation, compressed dispersion) has given way to a supply-driven scarcity regime driven by energy shocks, fiscal activism and the AI buildout, so bonds now provide income not duration diversification. The 60/40 should become a growth/AI core, income across public and private credit, and market-neutral systematic diversifiers, with systematic multi-strategy hedge funds at the core of the hedge fund book; AI bottleneck profits will dissipate but valuations are modest.

speakers.name: Mike Pile
speakers.role: Deputy head of BlackRock portfolio management group; ex-global CIO strategist; ex-US deputy national security adviser for international economics
speakers.speaker_note: Speaks for himself and uses 'we' for BlackRock's house view; corporate framing may soften risks. Caption spelling of surname.

worldview_premises.premise: Regimes differ by whether supply or demand dominates; 2010s were demand-starved, today is supply-driven scarcity (energy shocks, supply chains, AI buildout).
Stock-bond correlation depends on whether growth or inflation is the dominant risk; negative when growth dominates.
Policy pinned rates and QE pushed investors out the risk curve and suppressed both economic and market volatility.
Suppressed volatility compressed dispersion, shrinking the alpha opportunity set; the 2010s were poor for hedge funds because cheap diversification (long bonds) was abundant.
Zero rates rewarded long duration everywhere: long bonds, risk parity, long-dated cash flow tech growth.
Policymakers fight the last crisis: the GFC fiscal response was seen as too small, so large fiscal activism followed; the 2016-20 recovery reinforced this.
In the short run factors of production are fixed; in the long run they move to where the opportunity is, so bottleneck profits dissipate.
Breadth is key to active results (fundamental law of active management): breadth times forecast quality.
Pre-2007 quant strategies harvested factor exposures that drew down in stress; neutralising beta and known factors isolates alpha and is more resilient.
worldview_premises.support: BlackRock's quant-crisis experience; moderate stresses since

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Claims that factor-neutral systematic portfolios are 'more resilient' are asserted with no performance numbers.
The BlackRock house view sets growth equity as core and overweight US equities while also saying AI bottleneck profits dissipate; sizing is only 'appropriate'.
Direction of the real neutral rate is stated as unknowable, yet the near-term view is upward rates.
The claim that market-neutral strategies are best remaining diversifier is acknowledged as less straightforward than the 10-year Treasury but not quantified.
Hedge-fund resilience argument is by a BlackRock officer about BlackRock's own products.

forward_looking_inputs: Observable inputs: AI productivity data appearing in real time (earnings, productivity), duration of energy/supply shocks, fiscal deficits and capital-market demand, rate path and real neutral rate, equity dispersion and concentration. Horizon: quarters to years for bottleneck profits; medium-term for disinflation.
reader_inferences: Stock-bond correlation sign is a function of the dominant risk (growth vs inflation), implying a testable regime variable.
Sets dispersion and diversification scarcity as the two reasons for hedge fund demand.
